problem: Existing multi-agent cooperative navigation systems (e.g. Co-NavGPT) are vision-based and assume benign indoor settings, so they degrade under fire conditions (smoke, heat, sensor degradation, dynamic hazards) and ignore hazard exposure when planning.
motivation: Indoor fires make human access dangerous, and multi-agent search and rescue explores faster than a single robot. Smoke corrupts RGB/depth perception, causing missed and false detections, erratic exploration and paths through hot zones, so robust multi-modal perception and hazard-aware planning are needed.
key_idea: Fuse RGB-D, thermal and mmWave radar into a hazard-annotated global map, let a VLM assign risk-aware frontiers to the agents, and refine them with a hazard-modulated FMM local planner.
insight: The paper mainly diagnoses baselines rather than validating VULCAN: comparing normal and fire results shows that map-based methods (Greedy, Cost-Utility, Random Sample, Co-NavGPT) lose SR/SPL or explore less efficiently under smoke. Qualitative figures attribute this to three causes: perception failures (chair confidence drops 0.87 to 0.15, and a false toilet detection at 0.71), destabilised exploration, and unsafe hazard-blind routing. VLM-based planning (Co-NavGPT) gives the best SPL and the lowest cumulative hazard exposure among the baselines, which suggests semantic reasoning helps even without explicit hazard awareness.
method: Multi-modal perception and fusion: a VLM-based fusion operator combines aligned RGB, depth and thermal images into a 'smoke-transparent' image. An open-vocabulary detector and a class-agnostic segmenter then run on it, and pixels are back-projected with depth into 3D points carrying hazard attributes [temperature, smoke density, uncertainty].
Global hazard-aware point cloud: local vision points are merged with mmWave radar points across all robots, and DBSCAN removes outliers caused by flicker and smoke.

2D obstacle-hazard map and frontier risk: the 3D map is projected top-down into an obstacle map O and a hazard map H (weighted sum of T, S and sigma). Frontiers are clustered, given a mean-hazard risk score R_k and binned into safe, moderate or dangerous.

VLM global planner: a top-down rendered map with labelled robots and frontiers, plus a JSON per-frontier hazard report, is fed to a VLM that assigns one long-term frontier per robot, balancing low redundancy against low fire exposure and falling back to low-risk explored regions.
Hazard-aware FMM local planner: the FMM propagation speed is F(x)=1/(1+alpha*H(x)), so paths follow the negative gradient of the arrival-time field and avoid high-risk cells.
Fire-extended HM3D benchmark and CHE metric: smoke density, flame and visibility loss are injected into HM3D, and Cumulative Hazard Exposure (sum of H along all robot trajectories) is introduced.

setting.backbone: VLM global planner (Co-NavGPT-style, model unspecified) + open-vocabulary detector + segmenter + FMM planner; the reported results are for baselines only
setting.observation: RGB, depth, thermal imaging and mmWave radar (RGB/depth/thermal degraded by smoke in simulation)
setting.action_space: discrete: move_forward 0.25 m, turn_left/right 30°, look_up, look_down, stop
setting.simulator: Habitat-Matterport3D extended with simulated fire (smoke, heat); Gazebo used for qualitative sensor-degradation demo
setting.privileged: Global hazard map is used for CHE evaluation; the full VULCAN pipeline was not evaluated (end-to-end deployment ongoing)

numbers_note: The paper reports no quantitative results for VULCAN itself, only for baselines (Greedy, Cost-Utility, Random Sample, Co-NavGPT) in Tables 1 and 2, on a custom fire-extended HM3D set (36 val scenes, 200 episodes), so none are recorded. The table arrows in the fire table are also inconsistent.
results: Only baselines are evaluated. Under normal conditions Co-NavGPT has the best SPL (0.388) and fewest steps (185.43), while Greedy has the highest SR (0.686). Under fire, all baselines lose some SR (Co-NavGPT 0.666 to 0.660, Greedy 0.686 to 0.651), Co-NavGPT is again best on SPL (0.381), and it has the lowest CHE (4.873, vs 11.233 for Greedy). VULCAN is not quantitatively evaluated.
limitations: VULCAN's full pipeline is not implemented or evaluated; only baselines are tested, so the framework's claimed benefits are unverified.
Fire simulation is synthetic, HM3D has no human targets (objects are used as proxies), and there is no real-robot experiment.
Baseline degradation under fire is small in the tables, and the failure analysis is qualitative, based on single example figures.
